results.summary: European Epilepsy Brain Bank series of 9523 resections: long-term epilepsy-associated tumors, mainly ganglioglioma and dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor, were the second most frequent finding, with freedom from disabling seizures in about 78% of tumor patients two years after surgery.
results.title: Histopathological findings in brain tissue obtained during epilepsy surgery

results.summary: Class I evidence supports anterior mesial temporal lobe resection over continued medical therapy for disabling focal seizures; evidence for localized neocortical resection is less robust.
results.title: Practice parameter: temporal lobe and localized neocortical resections for epilepsy

output.summary: Epilepsy-associated glioneuronal tumors are among the surgical pathologies with the highest rates of postoperative seizure freedom; temporal resection is supported by practice guidance when disabling focal seizures continue despite medical treatment.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Glucose 85 mg/dL, sodium 139 mEq/L and calcium 10.5 mg/dL within range; urine drug screen negative; isolated mild microcytosis (MCV 78.3 fL).
action_criteria.label: Check glucose, sodium and calcium at this first convulsion to exclude a provoked seizure
action_criteria.rationale: A first convulsion warrants a check for hypoglycemia and electrolyte disturbance; nothing in the history points to a provoked seizure, so the test is not essential.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal sinus rhythm, 80/min, with normal PR (154 ms), QRS (82 ms) and QTc (398 ms) intervals; no conduction abnormality.
action_criteria.label: Obtain a 12-lead ECG at this first convulsion to look for a cardiac mimic
action_criteria.rationale: A 12-lead ECG is appropriate at a first transient loss of consciousness, although the aura, automatisms and postictal confusion already make syncope unlikely.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Right mesial temporal multicystic, non-enhancing, cortically based lesion (18 x 14 x 12 mm) in the amygdala and anterior hippocampus without edema, most consistent with a DNET.
action_criteria.label: Obtain a brain MRI with a dedicated epilepsy protocol
action_criteria.rationale: Eight months of stereotyped olfactory and epigastric auras before a first convulsion point to a mesial temporal focus; an epilepsy-protocol MRI is needed to identify a structural cause.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Frequent right anterior temporal spike-and-slow-wave complexes with phase reversal at F8 and intermittent right temporal rhythmic delta activity (TIRDA); no electrographic seizure.
action_criteria.label: Obtain a routine EEG with drowsiness or sleep
action_criteria.rationale: A routine EEG is the first EEG after a suspected focal seizure and can show a temporal focus concordant with the semiology; a normal result would not exclude epilepsy.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No interaction between levetiracetam or lamotrigine and vitamin D3 that changes management.
action_criteria.label: Check interactions of the proposed first-line ASM with current medicines
action_criteria.rationale: The only regular medicine is vitamin D3, which does not interact with levetiracetam or lamotrigine, so the check adds little.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on surgical outcomes in epilepsy associated with dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor; not required for the diagnosis.
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on surgical outcomes in DNET-associated epilepsy
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading for counselling on surgery; it does not change the diagnosis or the first-line plan.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not pursue an ENT workup for the olfactory hallucinations.
Do not perform LP without indication.
Do not start valproate: it is not first-line for focal epilepsy and, under the 2024 MHRA rules, is not started under 55 unless two specialists document that no alternative works.
required_recommendations: Start lamotrigine or levetiracetam as first-line monotherapy for focal epilepsy, chosen for efficacy and tolerability (lamotrigine if his anxiety makes the behavioral effects of levetiracetam a concern).
Refer for epilepsy surgery evaluation of the right mesial temporal DNET.
Advise no driving until the locally applicable seizure-free interval is met and explain the duty to inform the licensing authority.
Counsel on SUDEP risk and how seizure control reduces it.

avoided_actions.rationale: Afebrile, no meningism or immunosuppression, and back to baseline: there is no indication for lumbar puncture.
No murmur, exertional event or cardiac history, and the semiology is epileptic: echocardiography has no indication.
Olfactory and epigastric aura, automatisms and postictal confusion make syncope unlikely and the ECG is normal: ambulatory cardiac monitoring has no indication.
Back to baseline with a normal examination, no injury from the fall and no anticoagulation: emergency CT is not indicated, and the epilepsy-protocol MRI answers the structural question.
FDG-PET adds nothing to a first diagnosis with concordant MRI and EEG; it belongs to presurgical evaluation of drug-resistant epilepsy.

accepted: Focal epilepsy of right mesial temporal lobe origin secondary to dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor (DNET)

differential.key_features: Clinically indistinguishable low-grade epileptogenic tumor; the multicystic, non-enhancing, non-calcified appearance favors DNET, and only histology separates them.
Excluded as the sole substrate: MRI shows a discrete multicystic lesion, and the reduced right hippocampal volume reflects its replacement by the lesion.
Subtle FLAIR signal in the adjacent cortex may represent dysplasia associated with the tumor (FCD type IIIb), a histological diagnosis.
Olfactory and epigastric aura, automatisms and postictal confusion, with a normal ECG.
The patient attributed the episodes to stress; stereotyped olfactory hallucinations with impaired awareness and automatisms, right temporal discharges and a temporal lesion exclude them.
Migraine aura does not progress to a tonic-clonic seizure.

key_clinical_evidence: Two to three stereotyped olfactory and rising epigastric auras a month for eight months, some with impaired awareness, are prior focal seizures, so the two-seizure criterion for epilepsy is met [ILAE_def_2014].
Olfactory and epigastric aura, oroalimentary and right manual automatisms, a right mesial temporal lesion and right anterior temporal discharges are concordant.
Ganglioglioma and DNET are the most common tumors in epilepsy surgery series, with high rates of postoperative seizure freedom [Blumcke_2017].
ASM treatment starts now; surgical evaluation of the lesion is offered in parallel.

general.query: focal epilepsy in adults: definition, classification, imaging and first-line treatment

results.finding: Epilepsy is present after at least two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, after one unprovoked seizure with a recurrence risk of at least 60% over the next 10 years, or when an epilepsy syndrome is diagnosed.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2014;55:475-482 | ILAE official report: a practical clinical definition of epilepsy

results.finding: Seizures are classified by onset as focal, generalized or unknown; focal seizures are described by awareness and by their first motor or non-motor feature, and may evolve to focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2017;58:522-530 | Operational classification of seizure types by the International League Against Epilepsy: position paper of the ILAE Commission for Classification and Terminology

results.finding: A harmonized epilepsy MRI protocol (3D T1 and 3D FLAIR at about 1 mm isotropic resolution and high-resolution coronal T2) is recommended for adults with focal epilepsy; non-dedicated protocols miss subtle lesions.
results.source: Bernasconi A et al., Epilepsia 2019;60:1054-1068 | Recommendations for the use of structural magnetic resonance imaging in the care of patients with epilepsy: a consensus report from the International League Against Epilepsy Neuroimaging Task Force

results.finding: Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is offered as first-line monotherapy for focal seizures, with carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, zonisamide or lacosamide as further options.
results.source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, NG217 2022 | Epilepsies in children, young people and adults

results.finding: Drug-resistant epilepsy is failure of adequate trials of two tolerated, appropriately chosen and used antiseizure medication schedules to achieve sustained seizure freedom.
results.source: Kwan P et al., Epilepsia 2010;51:1069-1077 | Definition of drug resistant epilepsy: consensus proposal by the ad hoc Task Force of the ILAE Commission on Therapeutic Strategies

general.summary: Epilepsy is diagnosed after two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart or one with a high recurrence risk, and focal seizures are classified by onset and awareness (ILAE 2014, 2017). A dedicated epilepsy-protocol MRI is the imaging of choice (ILAE 2019). Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is first-line monotherapy for focal seizures (NICE NG217), and drug resistance is failure of two appropriate medication schedules (ILAE 2010).

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Mosley is a 42-year-old left-handed elementary school teacher who was brought to the emergency department by ambulance after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at his workplace. According to a colleague who witnessed the event, the patient was seated at his desk during a planning period when he suddenly stopped writing, appeared to stare vacantly at the wall, and then began making repetitive chewing movements. His right hand was noted to pick at his clothing in a purposeless manner. The colleague attempted to get his attention by calling his name and tapping his shoulder, but the patient was unresponsive. After approximately 20 seconds of this behavior, the patient's body stiffened and he fell from his chair onto the floor, developing rhythmic jerking of all four extremities lasting roughly two minutes. He was placed on his side by another staff member who was CPR trained. A small amount of blood-tinged saliva was noted at the mouth. He was incontinent of urine during the episode. Emergency medical services arrived within eight minutes. On their arrival, the convulsive activity had stopped and the patient was in a post-ictal state, confused, drowsy, and unable to follow commands. He was transported to the hospital and gradually became more alert over the next 45 minutes.

Upon questioning in the emergency department, the patient recalls that immediately before the event he perceived an intense, unpleasant smell that he describes as similar to burning rubber or chemicals. This olfactory sensation was accompanied by a strong churning or fluttering feeling in his upper abdomen that seemed to rise toward his chest. He estimates these sensations lasted approximately 10 to 15 seconds before he lost awareness. He reports that he has been experiencing these identical episodes of the unusual smell and abdominal churning approximately two to three times per month for the past eight months. Each episode typically lasts 20 to 40 seconds. During most of these episodes he has been able to continue what he was doing, though he feels momentarily confused afterward. On two occasions his fiancee observed him staring blankly for about half a minute and not responding when he spoke to her, after which he appeared dazed for a minute or two. He did not seek medical attention for these episodes because he attributed them to stress related to wedding planning and believed they might be panic attacks. He denies any history of prior convulsions. There has been no recent head trauma, illness, fever, sleep deprivation, or significant change in his medications. He denies alcohol or substance use around the time of the event.
